description: Solo developer from Ukraine building SEED, a Unity game for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. You are the surviving code of a crashed Mars probe: rebuild yourself from Martian matter, build an outpost and keep the crew alive through solar flares, dust storms and night. Mechanics are based on real NASA data (MOXIE, Curiosity RAD, Phoenix). Skills: C#, Unity, game design. Team is complete.
summary:
SEED is a Mars survival game for young learners, built in Unity. You play as the surviving 3% of a crashed probe's code: rebuild yourself from Martian matter, build an outpost, and keep a human crew alive through solar flares, dust storms, meteors and freezing nights.

Every mechanic is a real mission trade-off made tangible. Silicon becomes solar power, but Mars gets only ~43% of Earth's sunlight. CO2 feeds MOXIE-style life support, but only while there is power. Iron regolith shields the crew from radiation measured by Curiosity's RAD. Water ice is rare, as Phoenix showed. Players cannot max out everything at once, so they learn to prioritise like a mission planner.

Short NASA fact pop-ups appear exactly when an event hits, so the science arrives when it matters. The game has a 5-chapter campaign, an interactive tutorial and full EN/UK voice-over, which makes Mars mission thinking playable and memorable.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SEED is a Mars survival game that turns real mission trade-offs into gameplay. The player is SEED, the surviving code of a crashed probe. It rebuilds itself, builds an outpost and keeps a human crew alive until it can send a signal home.

HOW IT WORKS

- A 4-act opening cutscene shows the launch, the flight to Mars, the crash and the dark awakening.

- A 5-chapter campaign: Awakening (rebuild your core), Outpost (prepare modules before the crew lands), Glitches (fight corrupted code), The Long Storm (survive a global dust storm), Signal Home (collect beacon parts and defeat the final boss).

- Resources: Si gives power, Fe gives shielding, CO2 gives life support, H2O gives the greenhouse. Ice exists only in ice fields.

- Outpost modules: solar panels, batteries, radiation shelter, MOXIE, greenhouse and meteor defence.

- Mission events: solar particle events, dust storms, cold Martian nights, dust devils and meteor impacts with craters full of ore.

- Once the crew lands, oxygen and food must stay above zero and the radiation dose below the limit, or the mission fails.

- Progression: 8 levels with new abilities (dash, pulse, magnet, gun, shield, repair drone, boost) and 7 upgradeable skills.

- Learning: an 8-step interactive tutorial, Mission Control tasks, and short NASA fact pop-ups that pause the game exactly when the related event happens.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Young learners do not just read that Mars has weak sunlight, a thin CO2 atmosphere and dangerous radiation. They feel it: a dust storm cuts power, low power stops life support, and a solar flare forces a choice between shielding and growth. The goal is to build intuition for how a real Mars mission is planned, and curiosity to learn more.

CREATIVITY

The player is not an astronaut but the code that keeps astronauts alive. Losing data ("-12 B RADIATION") makes radiation damage visible and personal. A blue Martian sunset, real instrument names and mission history are woven into the story.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accessibility (EN/UK voice-over with 4 roles, three difficulty levels, keyboard/mouse and touch controls), pacing for short attention spans (hints only when needed, no timers on tasks), autosave and chapter checkpoints, and balance tested with bots on all three difficulties.

TOOLS

Unity (C#), procedural 2D graphics, Piper neural TTS for the voice-over, GitHub.
